title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
section: Exercise 1: Four groups at a glance
text:
Exercise 1: Four groups at a glance
wind has 100 rows: a region and a capacity_pct — the percentage of its theoretical maximum output that a site actually delivered.
Draw violins by region, ordered by median rather than alphabetically, and finish by printing the four group means.


















NoteHint 1





The violins are the Week 6 pattern with four groups instead of two — nothing changes.
The ordering is the new part. ggplot puts a character axis in alphabetical order, which here means “Northern England, Scotland, Southern England, Wales” — an order that hides the two clusters. You want the regions arranged by the thing being measured.
reorder(factor, values) reorders the first argument by a summary of the second. Its default summary is the mean; FUN = median orders by the middle site, which a few extreme sites can’t drag about.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(df, aes(x = reorder(group, value, FUN = median), y = value)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "...", y = "...")

tapply(df$value, df$group, mean)
Reordering inside aes() leaves the data alone and changes only the plot. That is usually what you want — the alternative, converting the column to a factor with explicit levels, affects every later use of it.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(wind, aes(x = reorder(______, capacity_pct, FUN = ______),
                 y = ______)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "Region",
       y = "Capacity factor (% of maximum output)",
       title = "Wind farm capacity factor by UK region")

tapply(wind$capacity_pct, wind$______, ______)











TipSolution





ggplot(wind, aes(x = reorder(region, capacity_pct, FUN = median),
                 y = capacity_pct)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(x = "Region",
       y = "Capacity factor (% of maximum output)",
       title = "Wind farm capacity factor by UK region")

tapply(wind$capacity_pct, wind$region, mean)
Two clusters, and ordering the axis is what makes them visible:

Higher: Northern England 29.9 %, Scotland 29.6 %
Lower: Wales 24.7 %, Southern England 23.2 %

That is geographically plausible — northern and western sites are windier. But the gaps are very different in size. Six points separate the clusters; three-tenths of a point separates Northern England from Scotland. The question is not “are the four numbers identical”, because four sample means never are. The question is which of these gaps is bigger than the sampling noise.
Note also that the violins are much the same height. ANOVA assumes roughly equal variance across groups, and you have just checked it without being asked to.





Extension: show the sites
Optional. ?geom_jitter, ?geom_violin, ?stat_summary, ?geom_errorbar.

Overlay the 25 individual sites on each violin. Does any region look like it has sub-groups within it? A bimodal region would make its mean nearly meaningless, and a violin’s smoothing can blur sub-groups away (or invent them); the points can’t.
Now replace the violins themselves with means and an approximate 95 % confidence interval, but keep the jittered points from step 1 showing behind them. That combination — raw points plus mean ± CI — is what ANOVA actually reasons about, and it is noticeably less reassuring than the violins: the points overlap heavily between regions even where the CIs do not. stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, fun.args = list(mult = 1.96)) draws it in one line (mean_cl_normal() would be the exact t-based version, but it needs the Hmisc package, which isn’t available here — 1.96 standard errors is close enough at 25 sites per group).
Add a horizontal line at the overall mean of 26.8 %. ANOVA compares the spread of group means around that line with the spread of sites around their own group mean, so this one line makes the F statistic visible.
Order the regions north to south instead of by output, and decide which ordering you would publish. There is a real argument for each.









Further reading: on why we don’t use box plots — they are harder to read than they look — and what to show instead — Nick Desbarats, “I’ve Stopped Using Box Plots. Should You?”, Nightingale, and Claus Wilke, “Visualizing uncertainty”, Fundamentals of Data Visualization, ch. 9.

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
section: Exercise 2: One test instead of six
text:
Exercise 2: One test instead of six
ANOVA compares the variation between group means with the variation within groups. If the group means are further apart than the noise inside each group would explain, F is large and p is small.
Run it, and print the summary.


















NoteHint 1





aov() takes the same formula shape as t.test(). The difference is what you do with the result: printing an aov object on its own shows you sums of squares and not much else, so wrap it in summary().
The degrees of freedom are worth a moment. One line of the table is about the regions, the other about everything left over. With four groups and 100 sites, you should be able to predict both numbers before you run it.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
fit <- aov(outcome ~ group, data = df)
summary(fit)
Save the fit to a name. TukeyHSD in the next exercise needs the aov object itself, not its summary, and re-running the fit there would work but would also invite the two to drift apart.











NoteHint 3





wind_aov <- aov(______ ~ ______, data = wind)
summary(______)











TipSolution





wind_aov <- aov(capacity_pct ~ region, data = wind)
summary(wind_aov)
F = 14.21 on 3 and 96 degrees of freedom, p = 9.8 × 10⁻⁸.
The degrees of freedom are 3 (four groups, minus one) and 96 (100 sites, minus four group means). If those numbers are not what you expected, something is wrong with the data before anything is wrong with the test — a common cause is R having read a grouping column as something other than four distinct values.
F = 14.2 means the group means are spread about fourteen times more widely than the within-region scatter would produce by chance. The p-value is tiny.
And it tells you almost nothing you can use. “At least one of four regions differs from at least one other” is not a planning recommendation. You already suspected it from the plot. What ANOVA buys is permission to go looking for the specific differences without the 26 % false-positive problem — which is the next exercise.





Extension: what ANOVA assumes
Optional. ?plot.lm, ?kruskal.test, ?oneway.test, ?bartlett.test.

plot(wind_aov) gives four diagnostic plots. The first two are the ones to read: residuals against fitted values (look for a fan shape) and a QQ plot of residuals (look for curvature). Does this ANOVA deserve to be trusted?
Run kruskal.test() on the same data — the rank-based version that assumes no normality. It gives p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶. Both are tiny, so the conclusion survives, which is the most useful possible outcome of a robustness check and the least reportable.
oneway.test() is the ANOVA equivalent of Welch’s t-test, dropping the equal-variance assumption. Compare its answer. Then work out from the group standard deviations why it barely moves here.
ANOVA with exactly two groups is a t-test. Confirm it: run both on Scotland and Wales alone, and check that F equals t².

title: Week 7: Comparing Groups
text:
Exercise 3: Which pairs actually differ?
ANOVA said something differs. TukeyHSD says what, comparing all six pairs while holding the overall false-positive rate at 5 % rather than letting it climb to 26 %.
Run it, then finish by printing how many of the six pairs are significant at the 0.05 level.


















NoteHint 1





TukeyHSD() takes the fitted aov object — not its summary, and not the data.
What comes back is a list with one element per grouping variable, named after that variable. Inside is a matrix with a row per pair and four columns: the difference, its lower and upper bounds, and the adjusted p-value.
Counting how many entries of a vector are below a threshold is a one-liner: a comparison gives you TRUE and FALSE, and sum() treats TRUE as 1.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
tukey <- TukeyHSD(fit)
tukey

sum(tukey$grouping_variable[, "p adj"] < 0.05)
The column is called p adj, with a space, so it has to be quoted inside the brackets. The comma before it means “all rows, this column”.











NoteHint 3





tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(______)
tukey_result

sum(tukey_result$______[, "______"] < 0.05)











TipSolution





tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(wind_aov)
tukey_result

sum(tukey_result$region[, "p adj"] < 0.05)
Four of the six:



Comparison
diff
p adj





Scotland – Northern England
−0.33
0.994
no difference


Wales – Southern England
+1.43
0.673
no difference


Wales – Northern England
−5.21
0.0005
differs


Wales – Scotland
−4.88
0.0012
differs


Southern England – Scotland
−6.32
<0.001
differs


Southern England – Northern England
−6.64
<0.001
differs



Every north–south pair differs; neither within-cluster pair does. The finding is not “region matters” but something sharper and more useful: latitude matters, and the distinction between Scotland and Northern England is not supported by these data. A developer choosing between those two on capacity factor alone would be choosing on noise.
One honest footnote. Run the six comparisons uncorrected and you get the same four. The correction changed nothing here, because these p-values are not close to the threshold. That is the usual case, and it is exactly why the correction is easy to skip: it looks like it never matters, right up until the study where your best pair sits at 0.03 and the corrected value is 0.18.





Extension: the correction, and what it costs
Optional. ?p.adjust, ?pairwise.t.test, ?plot.TukeyHSD.

Plot the Tukey result. Six horizontal intervals; the two that cross the zero line are the two non-significant pairs. Then work out why this figure is more use in a report than the table is.
Run pairwise.t.test() with p.adjust.method = "none", then "bonferroni", then "holm". Four comparisons stay significant throughout. Construct — or simulate — a dataset where they do not agree, which is the only way to see what the correction is for.
Corrections are not free: holding the false-positive rate down raises the false-negative rate. With 28 pairs instead of 6, how large would a real difference have to be to survive Bonferroni? ?power.t.test with a smaller sig.level will show you.
The deeper problem the correction does not solve: it assumes you declared your six comparisons in advance. Describe, in one sentence, how someone could run this exact analysis honestly and still end up reporting a false positive.











Quick check
With four groups there are six pairwise comparisons. How many are there with eight groups? Print the number.


















TipSolution





choose(8, 2)

Doubling the groups nearly quintuples the comparisons, so the false-positive problem grows much faster than the study does:




Groups
Pairs
Chance of at least one false positive at α = 0.05




2
1
5 %


4
6
26 %


8
28
76 %


12
66
97 %



At 12 groups you are essentially guaranteed a “finding”. This is the arithmetic behind the HolmesCo mineral survey, and behind a good deal of published science.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
text:
A model is a deliberate simplification: it captures some of reality and ignores the rest. The skill is not fitting one — lm() does that in eight characters — but knowing what yours has thrown away.
Today you will fit two models. One is honest about being incomplete. The other is HolmesCo’s, and it is about to be taken apart.
Goals:

Fit a linear regression and say what the slope means in words
Read residual plots for the structure the model missed
Rebuild a bad model and measure how much was being left out
See why a model that fits better can predict worse







NoteHow these exercises work





The code boxes start empty, except for comments to guide you through the code that’s expected.
Work one comment at a time. If you get stuck:

Hint 1 restates what you are trying to do.
Hint 2 sketches the shape the code might take.
Hint 3 gives you the code with the key pieces blanked out.
Solution gives you the lot.

Take a real attempt before opening a hint: you will learn by doing, not by reading. The demonstrators are here to help.
Three things worth knowing:

The boxes share one R session, exactly like a script. Anything you create in Exercise 1 is still there in Exercise 2.
Variable names are up to you. The last thing your block prints is what gets checked, so end each block with the answer.
Exercises have extensions underneath them. If you finish early, give them a stab. These are designed to equip you to tackle real coding problems you might face, using the documentation. We can help – but check the manuals first!

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
section: Exercise 1: Does heat help or hurt?
text:
Exercise 1: Does heat help or hurt?
solar holds 50 observations of panel temperature (°C) and electrical output_w (watts).
Draw the relationship: the points, plus a straight-line fit through them, properly labelled. Decide from the picture which way it slopes before you fit anything.















NoteHint 1





The scatter plot is the Week 2 pattern: data, an aes() mapping x and y, and geom_point().
Adding a fitted line is one more layer. geom_smooth() draws a trend through the points, but by default it picks a curved smoother, so you have to ask for a straight line explicitly.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
ggplot(data, aes(x = predictor, y = outcome)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(x = "...", y = "...", title = "...")
The grey band around the line is a confidence interval for the mean at each temperature — not a range the next panel is likely to fall in. Those are two very different things, and the plot does not distinguish them.











NoteHint 3





ggplot(solar, aes(x = ______, y = ______)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "______") +
  labs(x = "Panel temperature (°C)",
       y = "Output (W)",
       title = "______")











TipSolution





ggplot(solar, aes(x = temperature, y = output_w)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(x = "Panel temperature (°C)",
       y = "Output (W)",
       title = "Hotter panels produce less power")
The line slopes downward: output falls as temperature rises. That surprises most people, and it is real — crystalline silicon loses roughly 0.4–0.5 % of its efficiency per °C above 25 °C. A hot day brings more sunlight and a less efficient panel.
Look at the scatter around the line before you get attached to it. The points are spread widely at every temperature, so whatever this line is capturing, it is not most of what is going on. The next exercise puts a number on that.





Extension: what the line is hiding
Optional. ?geom_smooth, ?geom_abline, ?predict.lm, ?stat_summary.

Turn the confidence band off, then widen it to 99 %. Which version would you publish, and which would a manufacturer’s marketing department prefer?
Fit a loess curve instead of a straight line. Does the curvature it finds look like physics or like noise? Try changing span and watch the “finding” move.
Draw the fitted line without using geom_smooth(). You will need the model’s coefficients and a geom that takes a slope and an intercept. Doing it this way is more work and makes it much harder to plot a line that is not the model you reported.
Add a prediction interval — the range a new panel would fall in — alongside the confidence interval. ?predict.lm and its interval argument. The difference between the two bands is usually startling, and it is the band your reader thinks they are looking at.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
text:
Exercise 2: What the slope means
Fit the model properly, read its summary, and finish by printing the slope — the coefficient on temperature.
Then say the slope out loud as a sentence with units in it. If you cannot, you have not finished.


















NoteHint 1





lm(outcome ~ predictor, data = df) fits the model; summary() shows the table; coef() returns the coefficients as a named vector.
That vector has two entries. The first is the intercept, the second is the slope — so you can take it by position or by name, and by name is harder to get wrong.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
fit <- lm(outcome ~ predictor, data = df)
summary(fit)

coef(fit)["predictor"]
In the summary, read along the temperature row: estimate, standard error, t value, p-value. Then find Multiple R-squared lower down. A small p-value and a small R-squared together are entirely normal, and they mean “there is definitely something here, and it is not much”.











NoteHint 3





solar_model <- lm(______ ~ ______, data = solar)
summary(solar_model)

coef(solar_model)[______]











TipSolution





solar_model <- lm(output_w ~ temperature, data = solar)
summary(solar_model)

coef(solar_model)["temperature"]
The slope is −0.354: each additional degree costs about a third of a watt. Over the 37 °C range in the data, that is about 13 W out of roughly 250 — a 5 % effect, and consistent with the published temperature coefficients for silicon panels.
Three things in that summary are worth more than the slope:

p = 0.0015. The relationship is not a fluke.
R² = 0.19. Temperature explains 19 % of the variation. Cloud cover, panel age, angle, dust and inverter losses are all in the other 81 %, and none of them is in this model.
The intercept, 257.5 W, is the prediction at 0 °C — a temperature that appears nowhere in these data. Intercepts are routinely reported as though they meant something. Usually they are an artefact of where zero happens to be.

“Significant but small” is the most common honest result in science and the least often reported, because it does not make a headline.





Extension: the same model, interrogated
Optional. ?confint, ?predict.lm, ?scale, ?cor.

Get a confidence interval for the slope. Does it exclude zero — and does it exclude values you would consider practically irrelevant? Those are different questions and only the first has a standard test.
Re-fit with temperature centred on 25 °C — temperature - 25 inside the formula. The slope is unchanged and the intercept now means something. Which version would you report?
Predict the output at 60 °C. R will answer without complaint. Say what is wrong with the answer, and find the widest temperature for which you would defend a prediction.
R² for a simple regression is the square of the correlation. Confirm it with cor(), then explain why that stops being true the moment you add a second predictor.











Quick check
The solar model’s R² is 0.19. What percentage of the variation in output is left unexplained? Print the number.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
text:
Exercise 3: HolmesCo’s dominant control
HolmesCo monitored groundwater level and rainfall near a quarry for five years, 60 monthly readings. They fitted one model and wrote:

“Rainfall is the dominant control on groundwater levels (R² = 0.49, p < 0.001).”

Reproduce their model, then look at what it left behind. Residuals — the gap between each observation and the model’s prediction — should look like noise. If they have a pattern, the pattern is something the model does not know about.


















NoteHint 1





The model is the same call as Exercise 2 with different column names — groundwater level explained by rainfall, nothing else.
residuals(fit) returns one value per observation, in the order of the data, so it can go straight into the data frame as a new column. Then plot that column against month.
A horizontal line at zero is what makes the plot readable: without it your eye has nothing to judge symmetry against.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
fit <- lm(outcome ~ predictor, data = df)

df$resid <- residuals(fit)

ggplot(df, aes(x = time, y = resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "...", y = "Residual (m)")

summary(fit)$r.squared
Joining the points with a faint line makes a cycle far easier to see than the points alone. That is legitimate here because the x axis is time and consecutive points really are adjacent.











NoteHint 3





gw_model <- lm(______ ~ ______, data = groundwater)

groundwater$resid <- ______(gw_model)

ggplot(groundwater, aes(x = ______, y = resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Residual (m)",
       title = "What HolmesCo's model threw away")

summary(gw_model)$______











TipSolution





gw_model <- lm(gw_level_m ~ rainfall_mm, data = groundwater)

groundwater$resid <- residuals(gw_model)

ggplot(groundwater, aes(x = month, y = resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Residual (m)",
       title = "What HolmesCo's model threw away")

summary(gw_model)$r.squared
R² = 0.489. HolmesCo transcribed their own number accurately, and everything else about the sentence is wrong.
The residual plot shows two clear structures:

a 12-month oscillation — recharge is seasonal, and lags rainfall by a few months, which a same-month model cannot represent;
a slow downward drift across the five years, which in the full report is a “temporary pumping phase” mentioned nowhere near the conclusion.

So 51 % of the variation is unexplained, and that 51 % is not noise. It is two named physical processes. “Dominant control” is a claim about rank, and this model has never compared rainfall against the two competitors sitting in its own residuals.
This is the most useful habit in the week: a model’s residuals are where its next version lives.





Extension: the diagnostics R gives you for free
Optional. ?plot.lm, ?acf, ?cooks.distance.

plot(gw_model) draws four standard diagnostics. Work out what each is for, and which of the four would have caught the seasonal cycle. (One of them will not, because it does not know the order of the observations — and that is exactly why a residuals-against-time plot has to be drawn by hand.)
acf(residuals(gw_model)) plots autocorrelation: how strongly each residual predicts the next. A spike at lag 12 is a year. Find it.
Cook’s distance measures how much each single observation moves the fit. Which month has the most influence, and would you have guessed it from the scatter plot?
Now draw residuals against fitted values instead of time. It looks much healthier. Write one sentence explaining how a model can pass that diagnostic and still be badly wrong.











Quick check
HolmesCo’s R² is 0.489. What percentage of the variation in groundwater level does their model fail to explain? Print it.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
section: Exercise 4: Put the missing physics back
text:
Exercise 4: Put the missing physics back
You can see a season and a trend in the residuals. Add them to the model and find out how much they were worth.
A trend is easy: month is already a column, and adding it lets the model drift. A 12-month cycle needs a pair of terms — sin(2 * pi * month / 12) and cos(2 * pi * month / 12) — which between them can represent a yearly wave of any size and any phase. One term alone fixes the phase, and the phase is exactly what you do not know.
Fit it and print the new R².


















NoteHint 1





Extra predictors go on the right of the tilde, joined with +. You can write arithmetic directly in a formula, so the sine and cosine terms need no new columns.
Four predictors in total: rainfall, month, and the two seasonal terms.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
fit <- lm(outcome ~ a + b + sin(2 * pi * t / 12) + cos(2 * pi * t / 12),
          data = df)
summary(fit)
summary(fit)$r.squared
Why a pair rather than one term: a sine alone peaks in a fixed month. Weighted together, a sine and a cosine can peak in any month, so the model can find the phase rather than being told it. That trick is worth remembering for any cyclical data — tides, diurnal temperature, seasonal demand.











NoteHint 3





gw_better <- lm(
  gw_level_m ~ rainfall_mm + ______ +
    sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + ______(2 * pi * month / 12),
  data = groundwater
)
summary(gw_better)

summary(gw_better)$______











TipSolution





gw_better <- lm(
  gw_level_m ~ rainfall_mm + month +
    sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + cos(2 * pi * month / 12),
  data = groundwater
)
summary(gw_better)

summary(gw_better)$r.squared
R² goes from 0.49 to 0.88. Most of what HolmesCo reported as unexplained variation was a seasonal cycle and a downward trend, both visible in their own residuals.
The coefficients matter more than the R². The month term is −0.017 with p = 0.0001: the water table is dropping by about 0.017 m per month, a metre over the five years of record. That is the single most consequential number in the dataset, it is nowhere in HolmesCo’s report, and their model could not have found it because they never gave it a way to.
Two cautions now that you have a better model.
A rising R² is not proof. Adding predictors can only increase it, so a higher R² is evidence only when the new terms have a reason to be there. Here they do — seasonal recharge and pumping are physical processes someone named in advance.
And “dominant control” is still not established. Rainfall is still significant in the improved model. What has changed is that it now has competitors, and you can see their sizes. The original claim was not false because rainfall does not matter; it was false because nothing had been compared with anything.





Extension: how would you know you had gone too far?
Optional. ?anova, ?AIC, ?step, ?summary.lm for adjusted R².

Compare the two models with anova(gw_model, gw_better). What is the null hypothesis of that test, and why can you only use it on models where one is nested inside the other?
Compare adjusted R² instead of R². Then add three columns of pure random noise as predictors and watch the two diverge.
AIC() penalizes complexity differently again. Rank all your models by AIC and by adjusted R². Do they agree — and what would you do if they did not?
step() will search for a model automatically. Run it, then write down why letting an algorithm choose your predictors and then reporting the p-values it produces is a form of the multiple comparisons problem from Week 7.

title: Week 8: Models and Their Limits
section: Exercise 5: The model that fits better and predicts worse
text:
Exercise 5: The model that fits better and predicts worse
A more complex model always fits the data you already have at least as well. That is a mathematical fact about fitting, not evidence about the world.
Fit a 15-term polynomial to the solar data alongside the straight line, draw both, then ask each one what a panel does at 45 °C — just outside the range of the data.


















NoteHint 1





poly(x, 15) inside a formula fits a fifteenth-degree polynomial — fifteen wiggles’ worth of freedom for fifty points.
To draw a smooth curve you need predictions at many temperatures, not just the fifty you have: build a data frame of closely spaced temperatures and call predict() on it.
predict(fit, newdata = ...) is also how you ask a model about a value it has never seen. R will not warn you when that value is outside the data.











NoteHint 2





The shape of it:
simple <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
overfit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 15), data = df)

grid <- data.frame(x = seq(3, 44, by = 0.2))
grid$simple <- predict(simple, newdata = grid)
grid$poly15 <- predict(overfit, newdata = grid)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = simple, colour = "Linear")) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = poly15, colour = "Polynomial")) +
  labs(colour = "Model")

predict(overfit, newdata = data.frame(x = 45))
The grid column has to be named exactly as the predictor is named in the model, or predict() cannot find it. You will also want coord_cartesian(ylim = c(200, 300)), because otherwise the curve leaves the plot and takes the data with it.











NoteHint 3





simple <- lm(output_w ~ temperature, data = solar)
overfit <- lm(output_w ~ ______(temperature, 15), data = solar)

temp_grid <- data.frame(temperature = seq(3, 44, by = 0.2))
temp_grid$simple <- predict(simple, newdata = temp_grid)
temp_grid$poly15 <- predict(______, newdata = temp_grid)

ggplot(solar, aes(temperature, output_w)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = temp_grid, aes(y = simple, colour = "Linear")) +
  geom_line(data = temp_grid, aes(y = poly15, colour = "Polynomial (15)")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(200, 300)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Output (W)", colour = "Model")

predict(overfit, newdata = data.frame(temperature = ______))











TipSolution





simple <- lm(output_w ~ temperature, data = solar)
overfit <- lm(output_w ~ poly(temperature, 15), data = solar)

temp_grid <- data.frame(temperature = seq(3, 44, by = 0.2))
temp_grid$simple <- predict(simple, newdata = temp_grid)
temp_grid$poly15 <- predict(overfit, newdata = temp_grid)

ggplot(solar, aes(temperature, output_w)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = temp_grid, aes(y = simple, colour = "Linear")) +
  geom_line(data = temp_grid, aes(y = poly15, colour = "Polynomial (15)")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(200, 300)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Output (W)",
       colour = "Model",
       title = "Which would you trust at 45 °C?")

predict(overfit, newdata = data.frame(temperature = 45))
The polynomial has R² = 0.60 against the straight line’s 0.19 — three times the fit by that measure, and you need coord_cartesian() to see the data at all, because the curve leaves the plot near the edges.
At 45 °C the straight line predicts 241.6 W. The polynomial predicts about 67 800 W, from a panel rated at 250. Nothing objected.
Three things to take from this:

Fit and prediction are different. R² measures agreement with data you have already seen — the one thing you never needed a model for.
Extrapolation fails silently. The polynomial is unreliable inside the data too; outside it, it is absurd. A matter of degree, not kind.
This is HolmesCo’s groundwater extrapolation in a costume: a line fitted to five years, extended forward to predict an empty aquifer by

The model does not know what it is modelling.


The straight line misses plenty. It is still the one you would stake a recommendation on.





Extension: find where it breaks
Optional.

Refit at degrees 2, 5, 8 and 15, predicting at 45 °C each time. Where does the answer stop being physically plausible? There is no sharp threshold, which is itself the point.
Split the data: fit on a random 35 panels and measure the error on the 15 you held back. Do that for each degree and plot error against complexity. The curve should fall and then rise — that U is the whole of model selection in one picture.
Repeat task 2 with a different random split. How much does the best degree move? With 50 observations, rather a lot — which is why serious model selection uses many splits rather than one.
Fit the model physics actually suggests: output against temperature - 25, so the intercept is the rated output at the reference temperature. Compare its R² with the polynomial’s, then say why “it fits worse” is not the objection it sounds like.

text:
The biomass question
“Does UK biomass power help reach net zero, and should we keep paying for it?”
This week: explore the data. Get a feel for the numbers.

Next week: make proper figures and start making the case.


Don’t try to answer the question today. Today is about becoming comfortable with the data and with R.

text:
Open the course page

🖥️ Navigate to the Week 1 exercise page



[16:10–16:15] Get everyone to the page. Help anyone who can’t load it. Common issues: slow first load (WebR is downloading R packages), browser compatibility (Chrome/Edge best).

title: Meet the data (and Git)
text:
Loading the data










What are the columns?
What years does it cover?
What units are used?



[16:15–16:35] Live walkthrough — type this, don’t paste it. The students have the same file open on the exercise page; tell them to see whether they can beat you to it, and start typing after a minute so the slower ones can follow.
Anticipated code:
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")
head(elec)
Then show str() and nrow() on the same cell. Narrate: “This is like pd.read_csv() in Python. head() is like df.head().”
Point out: columns are fuel types, values are TWh.
If the cell errors on the path, the page is being served from file:// — it needs HTTP.

title: Meet the data (and Git)
text:
A first plot










“What’s the first thing you notice?”



total gen > sum(sources) because of unlisted “other”
Again, type it. Put the bare plot() up first, with no labels, and ask the room what is wrong with it before adding them.
Total generation, not bioenergy, so the students still have Exercise 2 to do themselves; the same plot() pattern carries over.
Anticipated code:
plot(elec$year, elec$total_twh,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total generation (TWh)",
     main = "UK electricity generation")
elec comes from the previous slide’s cell — run that one first, or re-read the CSV here.
Total generation peaked at 398 TWh in 2005 and fell to 294 TWh in 2025, down 26 %. Most students expect it to have grown.
Ask: “How does this compare to what you expected?” Then: “why might it have fallen?” (efficiency, less heavy industry, more imports).
Plant the seed for Exercise 5: any fuel’s share rises when the total falls, even if the fuel itself stands still. “Is that a big number?” comes next week.
Drax converted its first unit to biomass in 2013 and stopped burning coal in 2021; the UK’s last coal plant (Ratcliffe) closed in September 2024, so 2024 still shows 2 TWh of coal; DUKES 2026 leaves 2025 blank, which the course file records as 0.

title: Meet the data (and Git)
text:
Why Git?
Your code needs to be:

Saved — not just in the browser
Versioned — so you can go back if something breaks
Visible — so you can share your progress


Git does all three. GitHub Desktop makes it painless.


[16:55–17:00] Brief motivation. Don’t oversell Git — just frame it as “how professionals save their work.”

title: Meet the data (and Git)
text:
The workflow


Every session:

Open GitHub Desktop
Pull any changes
Do your work in .R files
Commit with a message
Push



That’s it.
Your commit history becomes your learning record.



Committing loads the van; pushing sends it to the depot.






Emphasize simplicity. Resist the urge to explain branches, merges, or anything advanced. Week 5 will cover collaboration.+
Committing is like loading your changes onto a removals van on your driveway.
Pushing sends the van to the depot – your changes are safe
Pulling delivers any changes from the depot to wherever you are working.

section: Hall of shame: the satisfaction pyramid
text:
Hall of shame: the satisfaction pyramid






Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026


Volume encodes nothing: the 45 % tier looks many times the size of the 22 % one. And “not happy” sits between happy and complacent.


[16:15–16:20 for the whole section] Before the session, open the Chart audit category and count posts per chart (titles start [Chart N]). Lead with the most-posted; skip any that drew nothing.
Ask the author of a good post to say what they spotted, rather than reading the critique off the slide.

title: Making the biomass case
text:
Hall of shame: two cubes






Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026


Two cubes the same size, for 32 % and 30 %. Where are the other 38 %? And only 14 428 of the 30 903 respondents answered.


The missing 38 % are neutral (15 %), somewhat unfavourable (15 %), very unfavourable (7 %) and not sure (1 %). They’re on the Dig deeper page.
Compared to what? “62 % like AI” means 62 % of those who answered this question, under half the survey.

text:
Hall of shame: the treemap






Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026


The parts add up to 296 %. Respondents could pick several languages, so these aren’t shares of a whole.


A treemap, like a pie, claims to divide one whole. Multi-select answers can’t. Same lesson as the double-counted pie in the content session.
Fix: sorted bars, each out of 100 %.

title: Making the biomass case
section: Hall of shame: the language pyramid
text:
Hall of shame: the language pyramid






Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026


52 % sits on top of 63 %, and the tiers shrink far faster than the numbers. A pyramid implies a hierarchy that isn’t there.


The five values span 52–63 %. The drawing turns an 11-point spread into a sliver against a slab.
Multi-select again: a pyramid of parts is meaningless when the parts overlap.

title: Making the biomass case
text:
The same data, done properly






Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026, Dig deeper: AI usage


Every answer shown, in scale order, every bar labelled, n stated. Their caption even says: “This is not proof … but they are certainly related.”


The two cubes, redrawn by Stack Overflow themselves one click away.
The quoted caption is about experience and favourability: correlation isn’t causation, and they say so. Credit where it’s due.
Segue: “Now make yours look like this, not like the landing page.”

title: Making the biomass case
text:
Live demo

🖥️ Building a multi-fuel line chart in WebR



[16:20–16:35] Build one complete ggplot on screen. Suggested plot: UK electricity by fuel type over time (line chart, colour by fuel).
Walk through: load data → reshape if needed (pivot_longer) → ggplot → add labels → add caption. Narrate each step.
Emphasize: “This is the kind of figure that goes in a policy briefing. Notice the caption tells the reader what to see.”

title: Making the biomass case
section: The anatomy of a good figure
text:
The anatomy of a good figure









Every figure should have a “so what” — what should the reader take from it?


Build this live, one layer at a time. Don’t paste it. The students have the same data open on the exercise page — tell them to see whether they can beat you to a legible four-fuel chart, and start typing a minute in so the slower ones can follow.
Anticipated code (the same solution as Exercise 1 on the exercise page, so the two agree):
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")

elec_long <- pivot_longer(
  elec,
  cols = c(coal_twh, gas_twh, wind_twh, bioenergy_twh),
  names_to = "fuel",
  values_to = "twh"
)

ggplot(elec_long, aes(x = year, y = twh, colour = fuel)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Generation (TWh)",
    colour = "Fuel type",
    caption = "Source: DUKES 2026 Table 5.6.B"
  )
Suggested build order: plot one fuel with geom_line() first, hit the wall of needing a second geom_ per fuel, then reshape. The reshape earns its place that way.
Show the completed plot. Ask: “What’s the story here?” Students should see biomass rising as coal falls.

text:
Work through the exercises

The WebR page has four main exercises with hints:


Trend plot — biomass over time, with context
Comparison plot — emissions per MWh by fuel
Import plot — pellet origins over time
Context plot — biomass as % of total


Extension: Can you make biomass look more important — or less important — than it really is?


[16:35–17:25] The bulk of the session. Circulate actively.
Common issues: wrong column names, wide vs long format confusion, forgetting to load ggplot2, aesthetic mapping errors.
The extension is a preview of Week 4. Don’t belabour it, but students who try it will be ahead of the game.

What does this figure show clearly?

[17:25–17:40] This is important: first time students see each other’s choices and recognize that the same data can produce different impressions. Primes Week 4.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Goals
In the content session, you audited the assumptions behind biomass carbon accounting.
Now: test what happens when you change them.

Add transport emissions
Add supply chain emissions
Change the forest regrowth timeline
See how wide the range gets



[16:05–16:15] Open WebR, recap. Today is scenario analysis — arithmetic with a purpose. The exercises provide the emission factors and distances; students focus on sensitivity, not data collection.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Starting point: the “official” view
Biomass emission factor at combustion: 0 gCO₂/kWh
(That’s the carbon accounting rule.)

But what if we add the costs the rule ignores?


[16:15–16:35] Walk through two additions live on screen.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Adding transport









How much does transport add?



The students have the same constants in front of them on the exercise page; tell them to race you. Type the numbered comments first, then flesh it out with code. Start typing after a minute or so, so the slower ones can follow.
Anticipated code:
# 2. How many *MWh* of *electricity* per tonne of pellets?

# 1 MWh = 3.6 GJ, so a tonne of pellets gives 4.7 MWh of *heat* —
# but only 36% of that is electricity
mwh_per_gj <- 60 * 60 / 1000

mwh_per_tonne <- pellet_gj_per_tonne / mwh_per_gj * plant_efficiency

# 3. kg CO₂ per tonne shipped  
transport_co2 <- 6000 * shipping_co2_per_tkm  # kg CO₂ per tonne

# 4. kg CO₂ per MWh
transport_co2 / mwh_per_tonne                 # kg CO₂ per MWh
The answer is ~17.6 kg CO₂/MWh.
Do the efficiency step slowly. 17 GJ is heat; only 36 % of it is sold as electricity.
Ask: “Is that a big number?” Against gas (360) and coal (910) it is small. Against the official figure of zero it is large.
Constants match students’ exercise code.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Adding the payback period
Trees absorb CO₂ as they grow. But how long does regrowth take?


Fast regrowth (10 years): biomass is roughly carbon-neutral over the short term
Slow regrowth (40+ years): biomass has a carbon debt for decades
Net zero target: 2050 — only ~20 years away



If the payback exceeds the policy horizon, biomass is not carbon-neutral when it matters.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
The same fuel, six answers


w03-payback-scenarios.R



Walk left to right. 45 = “Counting all the regrowth that we assume will happen over next 100 yr” Same fuel, same chimney, same megawatt-hour — 1060 kg of difference, all of it from what you decided to count.
The two right-hand bars exceed coal(!) Wood (lots of C-O bonds in cellulose – partly oxidized) carries less energy per C than coal (reduced; mostly C).
So the case for biomass rests on the regrowth bars on the left. Ask: what would have to be true for the 20-year bar to be the honest one? Who checks that the forest actually regrew? The answer is an assumption, not a measurement.
The 20-year bar lands at 365, essentially the same as gas. Worth saying out loud: on a 20-year view, the best case for biomass is “about as good as burning gas.”

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Exercises
The WebR page has four scaffolded exercises:

Transport scenario — estimate CO₂ cost of shipping pellets
Supply chain scenario — add harvesting, processing, drying
Payback scenario — plot cumulative emissions under different regrowth timelines
Extension: Best case and worst case — combine all assumptions



How wide is the range? What does that tell you about certainty?



[16:35–17:20] Main working block. Circulate. The emission factors and distances are provided in the exercises — students don’t need to research them.
Key learning: the answer changes dramatically depending on what you include. The “official” zero is one end of a wide spectrum.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Attendance

Show the QR from https://attendance.durham.ac.uk/mytimetable, then ← back to the task.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Key messages

The answer depends on which costs you include
The timescale matters — carbon-neutral over centuries, but not over decades
The “official” answer (zero) is a policy choice, not a scientific measurement



[17:20–17:35] Draw these out from the room. Students should feel the force of the ambiguity.

title: Changing the assumptions
section: And it’s even worse than that
text:
And it’s even worse than that


w03-energy-input.R



Government’s own model (Stephenson & MacKay 2014, DECC; the report that inspired this project). EIR = energy that is not biomass (gas, diesel, grid electricity) spent per MWh delivered, counted as primary energy, as the comparator studies do.
Worst case, Pacific Canada: 0.95 MWh in for every 1 MWh out. Why? Wet sawdust dried with natural gas, then shipped via the Panama Canal. Best case (25 %): residues that arrive already dry.
Ask: what does this do to the “renewable” label? We have been counting CO₂; this counts energy, and it points at the same stage.
“What assumptions are we making?” The top of the bar is one choice of drying fuel.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Drax’s own numbers


Drax Biomass Tracker, Oct–Dec 2025. © Drax Group plc



Launched by Drax in 2026. Tonnes at every stage, per quarter; click “CO2 emissions” for supply-chain CO₂ by stage.
Ask: who produced these numbers, and what might a transparency tool leave out? It promises fibre types (sawmill residue vs roundwood) but does not show them; certification reads near 100 % everywhere; its own disclaimer says the figures are not authoritative.
Supply-chain CO₂ is 64–70 kg per MWh for Drax (Q2–Q4 2025), close to the ~60 we assumed in with_supply_chain, with pelletizing the largest share (61 % in Q4).
Open it live in a browser tab if there is time.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
Whose pellets?


w03-drax-origins.R



“Compared to what?” The worst bar is about a tenth of Drax’s fuel; most comes from the US South (25–76 % on the energy-input chart).
Drax’s Canadian mills are in British Columbia and Alberta: the report’s “Pacific Canada”.

title: Changing the assumptions
text:
The ethical question

“If you were writing a policy briefing, which scenario would you present? Why?”

title: Changing the assumptions

Cast your vote

Activate the poll before showing this slide.
Most students will say “the full range” — but some will say “best case” or “worst case.” Both answers feed the traitor discussion in Week 4.
Don’t resolve the tension. Let students sit with the disagreement.



Think about this. You’ll be writing that briefing next week.


This is the pivot to Week 4. Some students will recognize this as the traitors’ dilemma — a faithful briefing presents the range; a misleading one cherry-picks. Don’t point this out yet.

Pick the figure that best makes your case.

Right-click it → Save image as…

You type
You get

text:
Three phases



Phase
Time
What




Write
45 min
Write your briefing, commit it


Review
30 min
Read two others’, file an Issue on each


Reveal
25 min
Who were the traitors?





[16:05–16:10] Orientation. Remind students of the briefing structure. Traitors know who they are. Everyone else: read critically.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Briefing structure reminder

Summary — the answer, up front
Evidence — figures from Weeks 2–3, with captions
Caveats — what depends on assumptions
Conclusions — your recommendation



Everyone writes in the briefing.md they started in Week 3, on github.com (pencil icon, Preview to check). New figures: right-click → Save image as… into figures/, then commit and push.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Writing block

You have until the clock says 50 minutes.



Reuse and refine figures from Weeks 2–3
The analytical work is done — this is about synthesis
Traitors: be credible, not cartoonish



Hard deadline: whatever is committed at minute 50 gets reviewed.


[16:10–16:55] Circulate for questions about content, structure, and R code. This is the main working block.
Traitors may need reassurance: “You’re not lying. You’re writing a technically sourced briefing that happens to cherry-pick.”

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Peer review assignments
Each of you has two repos to review.

Navigate to the first one on GitHub now.



[16:55–17:00] Hand out assignments. Two each, drawn at random — so some of you will get two traitors and some none. Don’t tell them that; if asked, “the draw was random” is the honest answer.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
One Issue per briefing
Not one per section. The Issue is a conversation — the author replies in it. Tick a box by clicking it, or by typing an x: - [x].

Clarity: Is the main message clear? Could a non-specialist follow?
Evidence: Are figures honest and well-labelled? Numbers in context?
Uncertainty: Are limitations acknowledged?

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Two answers a script reads
Verdict   FAITHFUL / SUSPECT
Argues    KEEP-OR-EXPAND / KEEP-ONLY-WITH-CCS / PHASE-OUT

Pick from the drop-downs. A script reads them — this is the vote.


Say it plainly: there is no separate poll later.
Repos accepted before 2026-10-05 have no Peer review form under New issue. Their reviewers copy the block from the Peer review template page and type one option under each heading; if that is mangled, the review still helps the author but vanishes from the class results.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Then two required paragraphs

Why I reached that verdict — point at a figure, a claim, an omission. Not “it feels wrong”.



What made me want to believe this — answer it even if you voted SUSPECT.



[17:00–17:30] Quiet, focused work. Circulate, and push hardest on the second paragraph — students skip it, and it is the raw material for the debrief.
Warn them their answers may be read out, unattributed.
At minute 80, run the harvester for the first time and keep the output. It is your fallback if the API stalls during the reveal.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Attendance

Show the QR from https://attendance.durham.ac.uk/mytimetable, then ← back to the task.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Nobody stands up
There are 93 of us. You don’t know whose briefing you read, and they don’t know you read it.

So instead: the class reads its own data.
Every verdict you filed in the last half hour is already counted.


Say this out loud early — it defuses the anxiety that has been sitting under the writing block all session.
No traitor is named, tonight or ever. Anyone who wants the credit can claim it themselves afterwards.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
What you believed





Actually faithful
Actually traitor




Voted FAITHFUL
correct
fooled


Voted SUSPECT
wrongly accused
caught





[17:30–17:33] Read the two off-diagonal cells first — they are the interesting ones.
“Wrongly accused” is usually bigger than students expect, and it is the honest briefings that looked deceptive. Flag it; you come back to it in two slides.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
The split that matters
Suspicion rate, broken down by what the briefing argued.



Were you tougher on briefings that disagreed with you?



[17:33–17:36] This is the payoff for making Argues a separate field.
Traitors were explicitly allowed to argue the popular conclusion by dishonest means. If those slipped through at a higher rate than traitors arguing the unpopular one, that is confirmation bias with the class’s own name on it.
Don’t soften it, and don’t blame anyone: every reviewer in the room did the same thing.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
The three that got away
The least-suspected traitor briefings. Anonymized.


Which techniques survived scrutiny?


[17:36–17:41] Pick one and dissect it against the teaching notes — the techniques you held back from the content session.
Credit the craft. These students did a hard job well.

title: Write, review, reveal
section: And the one you all accused
text:
And the one you all accused
An honest briefing. Most-flagged in the class.


What did it do that looked like deception?



[17:41–17:44] Usually: a missing comparator, an unlabelled axis, a confident sentence with no caveat. Nothing deliberate.
This is the richest slide in the deck. Honest mistakes and deliberate deception are indistinguishable from the outside.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
The question

Not “how did you spot them?”
“What made me want to believe it — even though I thought it might be a traitor?”




[17:44–17:50] Start by reading out four or five harvested answers. They are already written, so nobody has to compose an opinion in front of 92 people, and hearing someone else admit it first is what unlocks the room.
Steer away from “it was obvious once I noticed X”. You want the honest version: the briefing was good, and that is the problem.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
Add yours











PollEv.com/geol
text geol to 07480 781235





Open response, not multiple choice — the vote already happened in the Issues.
Leave the wall up while you talk. Late arrivals keep appearing and the room keeps reading them.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
How you find out
Your reviewers’ verdicts, and whether the briefings you reviewed were traitors’, will be posted as a comment on each Issue.

Not by anyone announcing it in here.


The staff script posts the closing comment after the session.
This is also the formative feedback loop closing: your written comment on each Issue goes in at the same time.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
The real lesson

Honest mistakes and deliberate deception can look identical.
The skills that help you spot a traitor also help you avoid being one by accident.



This is the emotional peak of Phase 1. Let it resonate.

title: Write, review, reveal
text:
What you’ve achieved
In four weeks:

Articulated a question
Explored data
Tested assumptions
Produced figures
Written a briefing
Reviewed someone else’s work


Phase 2 starts next week. Same skills. Your question.


[17:50–17:55] Celebrate the accomplishment. Phase 1 is complete.
Preview: “Starting next week, you choose the topic. Groups of 3–4. You’ll design the investigation, analyse the data, and write an individual report.”

By the end of today:

Your group is finalized

[16:05–16:15] Finalize groups. Any students without a group join one now. Distribute the full topic list with data source descriptions.

Phase 1 (individual)

Edit

Accept the assignment: group assignment
Clone the group repo
Create a branch: add-my-name
Edit team.md — add your name
Commit → Push the branch
Open a Pull Request on GitHub.com

Narrate each step. Show the PR interface on GitHub.
Emphasize: branches keep work separate until ready. PRs let teammates review before merging.

title: Planning your investigation
text:
Why branches?
Without branches: everyone edits the same files → conflicts.
With branches: you work in parallel → combine when ready.


Think of it like lab notebooks: everyone writes their own notes, then you compile the report together.

title: Planning your investigation
text:
Do it yourself
Each group member:

Clone the group repo
Create a branch with your name
Add your name to team.md
Commit, push, open a PR
The group merges all PRs



Raise your hand when your group has merged everyone’s PR.



[16:30–16:45] This will be messy. Expect confusion about branches, merge conflicts on team.md, and at least one group trying to push to main. GitHub will refuse — main only accepts approved PRs. That’s the learning.
Demonstrators prioritize groups who are stuck.

title: Planning your investigation
text:
The template

Draft your plan in research-plan.md. It has seven sections:

title: First tests
text:
The complete workflow

Load data
Visualize: histograms, violins
Check assumptions: shapiro.test(), QQ plot
Run: t.test(y ~ group, data = df)
Interpret: CI, effect size, plain English
If violated: log-transform or wilcox.test()











[16:15–16:35] Work through the full pipeline live in the cell — type it, don’t paste it. The list above is on screen for the students too: tell them they have the same information you do, and invite them to beat you to step 4. Start typing a minute in.
Example data is the borehole set from the Week 6 content session, so the numbers are ones they have already seen.
Anticipated code:
borehole <- read.csv("data/borehole_temp.csv")

ggplot(borehole, aes(x = formation, y = temperature_c)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_point()

shapiro.test(borehole$temperature_c[borehole$formation == "Stainmore"])
shapiro.test(borehole$temperature_c[borehole$formation == "Whin Sill"])

t.test(temperature_c ~ formation, data = borehole)

t.test(log(temperature_c) ~ formation, data = borehole)
The numbers, so you can narrate without reading them off: raw data gives t = 2.24, df = 47.2, p = 0.030, 95 % CI [0.86, 15.97], means 35.3 vs 26.9 °C. Shapiro-Wilk on Stainmore is p = 0.032 — the assumption fails. On the log scale p = 0.22 and the CI crosses zero.
Emphasize: always visualize before you test. Let the room reach step 4 and celebrate the “significant” result before you run step 3’s verdict against it.

title: First tests

If you haven’t seen the data, you can’t interpret the result.

title: Deepening your analysis
text:
Complete analysis in 10 minutes
Track A: ANOVA → TukeyHSD → η²
Track B: t-test → QQ plot → log-transform → Cohen’s d + CI










[16:15–16:30] Keep it brief. One complete worked example, typed live, not pasted. Pick whichever track most of the room needs. Students have the same arrows on screen — invite them to run ahead.
Anticipated code, Track A (the wind data from Week 7 content):
wind <- read.csv("data/wind_output.csv")

model <- aov(capacity_pct ~ region, data = wind)
summary(model)

TukeyHSD(model)

tab <- summary(model)[[1]]
tab[1, "Sum Sq"] / sum(tab[, "Sum Sq"])   # eta squared
Track A numbers: F(3, 96) = 14.2, p = 9.8e-08, η² = 0.31. Tukey gives two clusters — Scotland vs Northern England is the one non- significant pair (p = 0.99); every comparison across the north/south divide is significant. Read the two-cluster story off the adjusted p-values, not off the F.
Anticipated code, Track B (the borehole data from Week 6):
borehole <- read.csv("data/borehole_temp.csv")

t.test(temperature_c ~ formation, data = borehole)
qqnorm(borehole$temperature_c); qqline(borehole$temperature_c)
t.test(log(temperature_c) ~ formation, data = borehole)
Track B numbers: p = 0.030 raw, p = 0.22 on the log scale.
Students need maximum work time today — if the demo runs long, cut the effect size and let them compute it in their own analysis.

title: Fitting and breaking models
text:
Regression workflow

Fit lm(y ~ x, data = df)
summary() — coefficients, R²
plot(model) — diagnostics
Interpret: slope, R², residual patterns











[16:15–16:30] Keep it brief — but still type it, don’t paste it. Students have seen this in the content session, so this is the ideal slide to say “you have the same four steps I do; see if you can beat me to the R²” and start typing a minute later.
Anticipated code — wind plus solar since 2010, which is exactly the series Exercise 1 on the exercise page builds:
elec <- read.csv("data/uk_electricity.csv")
elec$renewable_twh <- elec$wind_twh + elec$solar_twh
recent <- elec[elec$year >= 2010, ]

model <- lm(renewable_twh ~ year, data = recent)
summary(model)

plot(model)
Numbers to narrate: slope 6.64 TWh per year, R² = 0.978, p = 4.7e-13, residual SE 4.86 on 14 df. “Renewables have added about 6.6 TWh a year since 2010, and a straight line accounts for 97.8 % of the variation.”
Then ask the Week 8 question: R² = 0.978 and the residuals still curve. plot(model) panel 1 is where that shows. A very high R² is not the same as a model that captures the process — which is the extrapolation trap the exercise page walks into next.

title: Fitting and breaking models

title: Fitting and breaking models
text:
UK renewable energy: 2010–2025

Everyone does this exercise, regardless of project topic.


The WebR page has scaffolded exercises:

Fit a linear model to the renewable trend. Plot it.
Extrapolate to 2040. What does it predict?
Fit an exponential model. Extrapolate to 2040.
Which is better? Is either plausible?
What is the model not capturing?



[17:00–17:25] Both models “fit” the historical data well. Neither predicts the future correctly. The linear model underestimates; the exponential overestimates absurdly.
Students should identify: planning constraints, grid limits, saturation effects, policy changes.

AI got it right

AI got it wrong

✗ Our dataset is the full population, not a sample.

title: AI as critic

What to look for
AI is good at spotting mechanical issues:

Missing labels, unchecked assumptions, formatting


AI rarely asks the hard questions:

“Is that a big number?”
“What is this model not capturing?”
Those are the habits you have learned.
